I apologize for the difficulties with the search tools. Let me provide an answer based on my knowledge of biochemistry:

Cyanides are known to be highly toxic compounds. Their primary mechanism of toxicity is through the inhibition of cytochrome c oxidase (also known as Complex IV) in the electron transport chain of mitochondria. Cyanide ions (CN-) bind strongly to the iron atom in the active site of this enzyme, preventing it from binding to oxygen. This blocks cellular respiration, preventing cells from using oxygen to produce ATP.

This is a classic example of enzyme inhibition, where the cyanide acts as an inhibitor of the enzyme's normal function. Cyanide doesn't just inactivate the enzyme (which would imply permanent damage); rather, it binds to the enzyme and prevents it from carrying out its normal catalytic function while the cyanide is bound.
